records.title: Confirm a suspend actually locked the screen, since a stalled lock latches as locked with nothing engaged
records.symptom: The lid closes, or the idle timer fires, or `omarchy system lock` is run directly, and the machine wakes straight to the desktop with no password prompt at all. `omarchy-shell lock isLocked` and `omarchy-shell lock status` still say the session is locked, and every lock request after that, from the idle timer, from a later lid close, from `omarchy system lock`, reports success while no lock screen ever appears again.
records.cause:
Confirmed by reading `shell/plugins/lock/Service.qml` on this machine, omarchy 4.0.2-1, byte-identical to the v4.0.2 tag at commit 346e69e1cec6c4e8924531874af6ba010a1bc99e. The shell's `locked` property at line 37 is true as soon as a lock is requested (`lockRequested`, set true inside `beginLock()` at line 135), before the compositor has confirmed anything. `requestSessionLock()`, lines 63 to 77, clears its own retry timer and marks the lock done the moment it asks Hyprland for the lock, at lines 75 and 76, rather than when Hyprland confirms it. If that one request is ever declined or simply stalls, nothing retries it and nothing times out. From then on the `lock` IPC method sees `root.locked` already true and returns `ok` without doing anything, lines 513 to 516, and `isLocked` reports `true` off the same latched property, lines 519 to 521. The idle service gates the screensaver on the same property, so idling stops producing a screensaver too. Only two places ever clear `lockRequested` again, `finishUnlock()` at line 151 and the compositor's own `onLockStateChanged`, and both need a lock Hyprland has already confirmed, so a stall that happens before that confirmation cannot correct itself.

`omarchy-system-lock`, called by the lid close binding and by Super+Ctrl+L, discards the reply from the lock IPC and always exits 0, so nothing downstream can tell a real lock from a latched one. `omarchy-system-sleep-lock`, run from the suspend path, polls the same latched status and by design gives up after its budget, 12 seconds on this machine's logind settings, and lets the suspend proceed anyway, since the alternative is a laptop that refuses to sleep inside a closed bag. The only signal on wake is a critical desktop notification.

Established in issue #10299, confirmed by an upstream collaborator who reproduced the exact latched state on a worker VM and traced it to the two lines above, open as of 2026-09-18 with no fix proposed. What makes the original lock request stall in the first place, a declined or slow response from the compositor, is not established there or here, and neither the reporters nor the reviewer could trigger it on demand.
records.fix:
No upstream fix exists as of 2026-09-18, `#10299` is still open. Because the latch reads back as an ordinary lock everywhere a script checks, treat `omarchy-shell lock isLocked`, `omarchy-shell lock status`, and a zero exit from `omarchy-system-lock` or `omarchy-system-sleep-lock` as unproven rather than as confirmation. Ask the compositor directly instead:

```bash
omarchy-hyprland-session-locked
echo $?
```

Exit 0 means Hyprland itself is holding an `ext-session-lock`, real protection. Exit 1 means it is not, whatever the shell reports. Exit 2 means Hyprland has not reached a lock check yet, for example right after a monitor change, and is not a verdict either way. Run this after any suspend, lid close, or manual lock you need to trust, and before leaving a laptop unattended on the strength of it.

If it reports not locked while the shell still claims otherwise, clear the latch with a shell restart:

```bash
omarchy-restart-shell
```

Read what this actually does before relying on it. It checks `omarchy-hyprland-session-locked` first too, and in this latch it gets the same not-locked answer you just did, so it will not lock the session for you. It only replaces the stuck shell with a fresh one that starts in the state Hyprland already told you was true. Lock again yourself once it comes back up:

```bash
omarchy system lock
```

and confirm with the same `omarchy-hyprland-session-locked` check that it actually took this time.
records.verify:
```bash
omarchy-hyprland-session-locked
echo $?
```

Exit 0 confirms the compositor genuinely holds the lock, the only state where the desktop is not exposed. Exit 1 or 2 means do not treat the session as secured.
records.danger: Do not mute or dismiss the critical "Screen did not lock before suspend" notification that `omarchy-system-sleep-lock` sends. It is the only signal this bug gives before a laptop that looked suspended turns out to have been sitting unlocked the whole time. `omarchy-restart-shell` also behaves differently depending on what `omarchy-hyprland-session-locked` reports at the moment you run it. When Hyprland believes a lock is already engaged, for example a stale locker left behind by a crashed shell, the restart re-locks the session for you and gives no way to unlock it again over ssh. Check that exit code first, and only run the restart from the machine itself when you cannot.

records.title: Know that a shell plugin runs unsandboxed with your full account access, not as a config file
records.symptom: Is it safe to add a shell plugin from GitHub. What can a plugin actually reach once it is enabled, and could a bad one get at passwords, ssh keys, or anything else the desktop session can touch.
records.cause:
Documented in Omarchy's own manual, `manual/32-shell-plugins.md`, and confirmed by reading `shell/plugins/README.md`, both at the v4.0.2 tag, commit 346e69e1cec6c4e8924531874af6ba010a1bc99e, matching omarchy 4.0.2-1 installed here. The whole Omarchy desktop, not only the bar, runs as plugins inside one long-lived Quickshell process called `omarchy-shell`. The bar, its panels, the emoji picker, the clipboard manager, the Omarchy menu, the lock screen, and the polkit agent that approves privileged actions are all plugins in that same process, first-party and third-party alike, with no distinction in how they load. A third-party plugin added with `omarchy plugin add <url>` is cloned into `~/.config/omarchy/plugins/<id>/` and, once enabled, runs as ordinary code inside that same process, with the same filesystem, network, and D-Bus access as everything else the session already has.

The manual states this plainly, at the point where a plugin is added: "Before it does anything, it tells you plainly that plugins run as arbitrary, unsandboxed code inside your long-lived shell process, shows you the URL, and asks you to confirm." And: "A plugin isn't a config file — it's code that runs for as long as your session does, with everything your user account can reach." That confirmation is shown once, at add time. Nothing re-confirms it later, and `omarchy plugin update` runs a plugin's new code the moment its fast-forward pull lands, on the same trust the first install used.
records.fix:
There is no setting that sandboxes plugins, because none exists, and Omarchy's own documentation treats that as the given rather than a gap waiting on a patch. What is left to control is which code gets into that process in the first place.

Read a plugin's source before enabling it, not only its README. `omarchy plugin add <url>` shows the clone URL and asks for confirmation, but it does not show the code, and `omarchy plugin validate <path>` checks the manifest's shape, not what the plugin does with the session.

Add without enabling anything unfamiliar:

```bash
omarchy plugin add https://github.com/<owner>/<repo>.git
```

Leaving off `--enable` lands the clone in `~/.config/omarchy/plugins/<id>/` so the code can be read before `omarchy plugin enable <id>` actually runs it.

Before running `omarchy plugin update`, read the diff it shows rather than accepting it on reflex. An update is exactly as consequential as the first install, run under the same account with the same reach.

Check what is currently enabled:

```bash
omarchy plugin list --json
```

and remove anything that cannot be accounted for with `omarchy plugin remove <id>`.

The `omarchy.` id prefix is reserved for first-party plugins, so a third-party plugin cannot claim it, but that only stops a name collision. It says nothing about whether an unreserved id belongs to code worth trusting.
records.verify:
```bash
omarchy plugin list --json
```

Shows which plugins are actually enabled right now, first-party and third-party together, so the unsandboxed surface being relied on matches what was meant to be installed rather than what is remembered.
records.danger: `omarchy plugin remove` deletes a git-checked-out plugin outright once removed (the upstream repo itself is unaffected), so removing a plugin that was edited locally without committing those changes loses them. Only a hand-made plugin folder with no git repo is preserved, moved to a timestamped backup inside the plugins directory instead of being deleted.
